books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1861. Public domain. Wording verified against the Teaching American History text (teachingamericanhistory.org/document/first-inaugural-address-6/) and the Senate document (govinfo.gov, S. Doc. 62-439). The two passages appear in this order in the address; '. . .' marks omitted text.
stimulus.text:
Apprehension seems to exist among the people of the Southern States that by the accession of a Republican Administration their property and their peace and personal security are to be endangered. There has never been any reasonable cause for such apprehension. . . . I do but quote from one of those speeches when I declare that “I have no purpose, directly or indirectly, to interfere with the institution of slavery in the States where it exists. I believe I have no lawful right to do so, and I have no inclination to do so.”

. . .

In your hands, my dissatisfied fellow-countrymen, and not in mine, is the momentous issue of civil war. The Government will not assail you. You can have no conflict without being yourselves the aggressors. . . . We are not enemies, but friends. We must not be enemies. Though passion may have strained, it must not break our bonds of affection. The mystic chords of memory . . . will yet swell the chorus of the Union, when again touched, as surely they will be, by the better angels of our nature.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: A Southerner reading the second passage in March 1861 would most likely have understood Lincoln to mean that

options.text: the Union would be dissolved peacefully.
options.misconception: The passage speaks of “the chorus of the Union,” not of dissolving it.

options.text: the North would pay the South to return.
options.misconception: The passage offers no payment or bargain; it offers affection and a warning.

options.text: war would come only if the South chose it.
slavery would be protected in the territories.
options.misconception: The first passage protects slavery only where it already exists, not in the territories.

rationales.A: The passage speaks of “the chorus of the Union,” not of dissolving it.
rationales.B: The passage offers no payment or bargain; it offers affection and a warning.
rationales.C: “You can have no conflict without being yourselves the aggressors” tells the South that peace holds unless it strikes first. Background: Lincoln was setting the terms so that any war would begin as Southern aggression.
rationales.D: The first passage protects slavery only where it already exists, not in the territories.
rationales.general:
1. “In your hands” makes the South the decider.
2. “The Government will not assail you” promises no first strike.
3. Background: Lincoln's cabinet was split over Fort Sumter, and he needed the Confederacy to fire first.
4. The passage is less a promise of peace than a transfer of blame.
Remember: “you can have no conflict without being yourselves the aggressors” is a warning wearing the clothes of a promise.
